outcome: No proof, disproof or accepted resolution of the infinitude of prime quadruplets appeared between 26 Jan 2024 and 11 Oct 2026. The quadruplet-specific items are a finite 2026 census (Chen, Zenodo), a 2026 conditional implication (Choudhury and Wei, arXiv:2606.10331) and older unrefereed claims (Liberati 2015; Tan 2011 inside a Collatz paper). The large 2026 activity is on consecutive-prime gaps (H1 moved to 240, 236, 212 and 186, two of them credited to AI systems), and none of it addresses the pattern {p, p+2, p+6, p+8}.
problem_asks: One question: are there infinitely many primes p such that p, p+2, p+6 and p+8 are all prime (infinitely many prime quadruplets {p, p+2, p+6, p+8})? The statement asks only for infinitude. It asks for no density, no asymptotic count (the Hardy-Littlewood prediction is context, not asked), no size bound and no other admissible pattern. The definition used is the standard one (Wikipedia, 'Prime quadruplet': four primes p, p+2, p+6, p+8). The frozen revision says only 'prime quadruplets', so the pattern is read as that standard one.

events.what_happened: Tony Forbes, 'Large prime quadruplets', The Mathematical Gazette 84(501), Nov 2000, pp. 447-452. It gives early examples and states the partial result that there exist infinitely many primes p such that (p+2)(p+6)(p+8) has at most 14 prime factors. It adds that the quadruplet conjecture would follow if '14' could be reduced to '3', which 'seems be a problem of extreme difficulty', and it says the quadruplet sequence is conjectured to go on for ever. The article does not, in the part read, attribute the 14-factor result to a named author. The origin of that result is not established here, so the date below is the earliest source found.
events.delivers: Partial result only: infinitely many primes p for which (p+2)(p+6)(p+8) has at most 14 prime factors. This is almost-primality of the three shifted values, not primality of all four, so it is not a result on the bullet.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks: infinitude of primes p with p, p+2, p+6, p+8 all prime. The article itself says the conjecture needs '14' reduced to '3'.
events.time_since_posted: about 25 years; the note does not claim to settle the question
events.direction: Partial, and in the conjecture's favour only in the weak sense that it is a partial result. It neither proves nor cuts against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Shan-Guang Tan, 'On the solution of the Collatz problem', arXiv:1110.3465 [math.GM]. The arXiv abstract claims a proof that every Collatz sequence returns to 1. A search excerpt of the PDF shows a section titled 'Theorem of prime quadruplets' asserting infinitely many prime quadruplets. The excerpted proof asserts that quadruplets exist in every region without justifying that step. The arXiv abstract page does not mention quadruplets. The PDF body could not be read, so the section and its step come from the search excerpt only.
events.revisions: v1 16 Oct 2011; v2 31 Oct 2011; v3 11 Nov 2011; v19 20 May 2016; v20 16 Jun 2023; v32 29 Dec 2025 (arXiv version history). The version in which the quadruplet section first appeared is not established.
events.delivers: Claims (in a section of a paper about the Collatz problem) that there are infinitely many prime quadruplets. Scope matches the bullet exactly if the claim is sound.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim is sound. The excerpted step is unjustified, and no reviewer was found.
events.time_since_posted: about 14 years for the first version; no review found in any version
events.doubts: The same paper claims to solve the Collatz problem, which is an open problem, and is a math.GM preprint revised 32 times. The quadruplet section's step is, in the excerpt, asserted without justification. The arXiv listing shows no journal reference.
events.direction: Claims the whole bullet, answering 'yes'.

events.what_happened: James Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes', arXiv:1311.4600, posted 19 Nov 2013 (v3 28 Oct 2019), published in Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015). The abstract, read through a tool summary, says the method shows 'for each k, the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples', and gives liminf (p_{n+m} - p_n) finite for every m and liminf (p_{n+1} - p_n) at most 600. A search excerpt of the body says the positive-proportion statement means that for infinitely many n only some of the n+h values are prime, and that when k > 1 no case of the prime k-tuples conjecture is known. The paper body was not read.
events.revisions: v1 19 Nov 2013; v2 20 Nov 2013; v3 28 Oct 2019 ('25 pages; corrected typos'). Annals of Mathematics 181 (2015) is the journal version of the same work.
events.delivers: Positive-proportion statement about large admissible k-tuples: infinitely many n at which some, not all, of the forms are prime, for a positive proportion of such tuples. It names no specific tuple, so it does not reach {0,2,6,8}. The literal abstract sentence ('the prime k-tuples conjecture holds') is ambiguous about 'all' versus 'some'; see doubts.
events.remains: The infinitude of n at which all four of n, n+2, n+6, n+8 are prime, for the tuple {0,2,6,8}, which is the whole of problem_asks.
events.doubts: The ambiguity in 'holds for a positive proportion' is the only doubt recorded here, because the body was not read. The Baghdad Science Journal 2024 paper (mor-gupta-2024-positive-proportion-claim) repeats the phrase and reads it as a claim about all forms being prime, which would be far stronger than the 'some, not all' reading in the search excerpt. Which reading is right needs the body of Maynard's paper.
events.direction: Weak form: a positive proportion of admissible tuples have infinitely many n with several (not all) forms prime. Does not prove the conjecture for any given tuple.

events.what_happened: Diego Liberati, CNR IRIS repository records dated 2015, including one titled 'There are infinitely many quadruples of primes' (handle 20.500.14243/295044 per the search result, not confirmed because the page returned HTTP 403). Per the search snippet its abstract says a proof of the conjecture is offered and that the twin prime conjecture would follow. The same author has other 2015 records claiming proofs of the twin prime conjecture, of infinitely many sextuplets and of infinitely many primes n^2+1 (search snippets only).
events.delivers: Claims the whole bullet, answering 'yes'. The argument is not visible: the snippet says no files are attached to the record.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claim is sound. No text of the argument was read.
events.doubts: No full text is attached per the search snippet. The same author's records claim proofs of several open problems at once (twin primes, n^2+1, quadruplets, sextuplets), per the search snippets. No peer review or expert reading was found.
events.direction: Claims the whole bullet, answering 'yes'.

events.what_happened: Laszlo Toth, 'On the asymptotic density of prime k-tuples and a conjecture of Hardy and Littlewood', Computational Methods in Science and Technology 25(3), 2019, pp. 143-148 (arXiv:1910.02636 per Wikipedia). It finds Skewes numbers for eight further prime k-tuples and gives numerical data in support of the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. Wikipedia cites it for a quadruplet Skewes number of 1172531.
events.delivers: Numerical support for the Hardy-Littlewood asymptotic; does not prove the conjecture or any case of it.

checked_by.who: Computational Methods in Science and Technology (journal)
checked_by.qualification: journal of record for the paper

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (numerical); cuts neither way on infinitude.

events.what_happened: Ashish Mor and Surbhi Gupta, 'On Existence of Prime K-Tuples Conjecture for Positive Proportion of Admissible K-Tuples', Baghdad Science Journal (vol. 21, issue 3, a 2024 issue per the journal URL). Per search excerpts it claims that the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples and describes this as unconditional. The journal page could not be reached (DNS failure), so this is recorded from search excerpts only.
events.delivers: As excerpted, a claim of the positive-proportion form for all-prime admissible k-tuples. Neither the excerpt nor the search summary names the tuple {0,2,6,8}.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks. If the claim were read literally it would cover this bullet only as a proportion statement, which names no specific tuple.
events.doubts: If read literally (all k forms prime for a positive proportion of admissible tuples), the claim is far stronger than Maynard's theorem as stated in Maynard's abstract. The likelier explanation is a misreading of Maynard's 'holds' phrasing, but the paper was not read. The month is not established, so it is unknown whether the paper falls before 26 Jan 2024.
events.direction: As excerpted, a claim favouring the conjecture for a positive proportion of tuples; cuts neither way on this tuple.

events.what_happened: Akos Magyar and Janos Pintz, 'On the frequency of small gaps between the primes', arXiv:2505.07630, submitted 12 May 2025. The abstract says that Friedlander's near-precise answer on reciprocal sums of prime gaps relied on a generalized Hardy-Littlewood k-tuple hypothesis, and that the authors give an unconditional answer to a much weaker form of the same problem.
events.delivers: An unconditional result on a weaker form of a question about reciprocal sums of prime gaps. It is not about the simultaneous primality of any tuple.
events.direction: Neither way on the bullet; the hypothesis it avoids is a k-tuple hypothesis, so it is a neighbour, not an instance.

events.what_happened: Trey Smith, 'A Generalized Elliott-Halberstam Conjecture Implying the Twin Prime Hypothesis', arXiv:2511.14810, submitted 17 Nov 2025. It proposes a generalization of Elliott-Halberstam called GEH-2 and shows that GEH-2 implies the twin prime conjecture. It discusses consequences for prime gaps and k-tuple patterns.
events.delivers: Conditional: GEH-2 implies the twin prime conjecture. Nothing unconditional, and nothing about quadruplets.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks, and GEH-2 itself is unproven per the source.
events.doubts: The result is conditional on a conjecture the paper proposes. The abstract page gives no evidence that GEH-2 has been established.
events.direction: Conditional implication for the twin-prime case; neither way on quadruplets.

events.what_happened: Zhu (first name given as Li in one bibliographic record), 'Almost prime triples and Chen's theorem', International Journal of Number Theory 21(1), 2025, p. 133 (DOI 10.1142/S1793042125500071 per an EBSCO record). It proves infinitely many primes p such that p+2 has at most two prime factors and p+6 has at most 11. Per a 2025 arXiv paper cited in the search, it improves Cai's 2017 bound of 14 for p+6. Not opened; the EBSCO record and secondary citation were read.
events.delivers: Almost-prime (not prime) statement about the pair p+2, p+6. It is not a statement that p+2 and p+6 are prime, and it says nothing about p+8.
events.doubts: Read from a bibliographic record and a secondary citation, not the paper.
events.direction: Weaker than primality for the pair; neither way on the bullet.
people: Li Zhu (first name per one bibliographic record; to be checked)

events.what_happened: Kyle Pratt, 'The irrationality of a prime factor series under a prime tuples conjecture', arXiv:2409.15185, submitted 23 Sep 2024. Title and listing only; not opened.
events.delivers: Per its title, conditional on a prime tuples conjecture; about irrationality of a prime-factor series. Not a result on infinitude.
events.doubts: Not read; the conditional reading comes from the title only.
events.direction: Conditional; neither way on the bullet.

events.what_happened: William Banks and Kevin Ford, 'Sets of integers satisfying Bateman-Horn statistics', arXiv:2605.01155, submitted 1 May 2026. It proves that certain random sets of integers almost surely satisfy the Bateman-Horn asymptotics in full generality.
events.delivers: An unconditional probabilistic theorem about random sets. It is not a proof of Bateman-Horn for any specific tuple, and it does not concern quadruplets.
events.direction: Neither way on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Manik Kakkar, 'Neural Prime Sieves: Density-Driven Generalization and Empirical Evidence for Hardy-Littlewood Asymptotics', arXiv:2604.02383, submitted 1 Apr 2026. It trains a model called PrimeFamilyNet to learn probabilistic filters for seven prime families (twin, Sophie Germain, safe, cousin, sexy, Chen, isolated), trained on primes from 10^7 to 10^9 and evaluated up to 10^16. The paper describes its results as 'corroborating Hardy-Littlewood k-tuple predictions'. Quadruplets are not among the families.
events.delivers: Empirical search-space pruning for seven prime families. It is not a proof and it does not address quadruplets.
events.doubts: Empirical evidence only, as the title and abstract say. Recorded for the AI search: the system is a neural network built by the author, not a lab model.
events.direction: Empirical; consistent with the Hardy-Littlewood predictions; cuts neither way on infinitude.

systems.name: PrimeFamilyNet
systems.what_it_did: A neural network the author built to learn probabilistic filters for seven prime families. It is an empirical search-space tool and produces no proof. It is not a lab model and carries no release date.
systems.basis_quote: a multi-head residual network conditioned on the backward prime gap and modular primorial residues of a known prime $p$

events.what_happened: Himaghna Roy Choudhury and Shicheng Wei, 'Prime Quadruplets and Jump Conditions on Arithmetic Functions', arXiv:2606.10331 (math.NT). It studies composite n with phi(n+12) = phi(n) + 12 and sigma(n+12) = sigma(n) + 12. Prime quadruplets (p, p+2, p+6, p+8) give solutions n = p(p+8). The abstract claims that the characterisation is complete when n and n+12 are both squarefree semiprimes, that no solution is a prime power, and that a computer search to 10^12 found no counterexample. The authors conjecture that the only solutions are the quadruplet ones.
events.revisions: v1 9 Jun 2026 02:25 UTC; v2 12 Jun 2026; v3 22 Jul 2026; v4 15 Sep 2026 (arXiv version history). Some search summaries give 8 June, the US-local date of the same submission.
events.delivers: A characterisation for squarefree semiprimes, and a conditional implication: if the authors' conjecture (the only solutions are the quadruplet ones) holds and there are infinitely many solutions, then there are infinitely many prime quadruplets. It establishes neither premise. The implication is in the direction of the conjecture, but only conditionally.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks. The conditional premises are the characterisation conjecture and the infinitude of its solutions, both open per the paper.
events.doubts: The authors themselves call the characterisation an open conjecture. The abstract page was read; the PDF was not.
events.direction: Conditional implication in the direction of 'yes'; no unconditional result.

events.what_happened: Ruqing Chen, 'A Complete Census of Prime Quadruplets for Q(n) = n^47 - (n-1)^47 in the Range 1 <= n <= 2x10^11', Zenodo record 18728540, sole listed creator, version v1 dated 22 Feb 2026 (Synapse listing 24 Feb 2026). It reports 742 quadruplets, 7 quintuplets and 0 sextuplets for the polynomial over that range, with members of 340 to 520 digits, and a mod-3 identity. It presents itself as Part II of a project whose Part I is Zenodo record 18701355, which was not checked.
events.revisions: v1 22 Feb 2026 (Zenodo). Synapse lists the same work on 24 Feb 2026.
events.delivers: A finite computational census over one polynomial's values for n up to 2x10^11. It says nothing about infinitude. Whether its quadruplets are the standard {p, p+2, p+6, p+8} pattern in the bullet's sense is not established from the record, since they are described as values of a degree-46 polynomial. The mod-3 identity follows from Fermat's little theorem.
events.directly_checkable: In principle each reported quadruplet can be checked with a primality test. The list of quadruplets was not read, and the census method was not checked.
events.doubts: Single author, affiliated with a company (GUT Geoservice Inc.) rather than a research institution, per the Zenodo record. Zenodo preprint with no review. The Synapse listing garbles the author's name ('Ruqing Chen (Sun,)'), and a related Zenodo record names a GitHub handle Ruqing1963 (search snippet). Its claimed agreement with the Bateman-Horn conjecture is self-assessed. The mod-3 claim is presented as a result but is elementary.
events.direction: Finite census; neither way on infinitude.
events.object: The census itself: 742 quadruplets (members 340-520 digits) found by searching the values of Q(n) = n^47 - (n-1)^47 for 1 <= n <= 2x10^11, with 7 quintuplets and no sextuplets. Explicit but finite, and not individually listed in the record read.

events.what_happened: OpenAI preprint 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' (PDF on cdn.openai.com; dated 30 Aug 2026 per the PDF date in search and per the tracker; announced 3 Sept 2026 per Science News and the tracker). It claims liminf (p_{n+1} - p_n) at most 186, via DHL[40,2] and a multidimensional Selberg sieve, using equidistribution estimates of Polymath 8a and Stadlmann together with 'complementary factorization conditions'. A companion preprint 'Improved Long Gaps Between Primes' concerns lower bounds for maximal gaps; it was not opened. The Lean 4 repository openai/PrimeGaps186 (Apache-2.0) gives a conditional formalisation: three named project axioms (a rank-three hyper-Kloosterman bound attributed to Deligne/Katz, a rank-two Kloosterman correlation bound attributed to Fouvry-Kowalski-Michel, and 104 outer and 45 inner physical-integral bounds plus three cap bounds), with the numerical bounds checked by a Python/FLINT certificate outside Lean. Science News reports the paper was released 3 Sept 2026 and that OpenAI used a related largest-gaps problem as a benchmark for its newest model.
events.revisions: Single version found. The PDF is dated 30 Aug 2026; release is 3 Sept 2026 per two secondary sources.
events.delivers: A bound on consecutive-prime gaps: infinitely many n with p_{n+1} - p_n at most 186, conditional on the three axioms. It concerns gaps between consecutive primes, not the simultaneous primality of p, p+2, p+6, p+8, so it does not establish any count of primes in the pattern {0,2,6,8}.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks. The result addresses consecutive-prime gaps, not all four forms of {0,2,6,8}.

events.doubts: (1) The Lean result verifies only the consequence of three input axioms, not the axioms themselves; the repository says so. (2) The numerical integral and cap bounds are checked outside Lean. (3) No referee report or independent expert verification was found. (4) Terence Tao criticised the approach in a Mathstodon post, reported by Science News, as 'a consequence of some very deliberate choices to abandon any pretense of gaining human understanding'. That is a criticism of method, not a finding on correctness. (5) Science News reports mathematicians were still 'digesting' the paper. (6) Conduct dispute with Stadlmann (see disputes). The sorry count of the Lean development was not stated in the README read.
events.direction: Improves the consecutive-gap bound. Relative to the bullet it is orthogonal: no statement about quadruplets.

A claim that the model found the factorisation conditions is attributed to a public post by Weijie Su, which I could not locate, so it is not recorded as a fact.

events.what_happened: Julia Stadlmann, 'Bounded gaps between primes', arXiv:2608.31126 (math.NT), a single version posted 31 Aug 2026. It proves H1 at most 240, improving Polymath 8b's 246, by combining Bombieri-Vinogradov with newer equidistribution estimates for smooth moduli. The summary of the paper says the computation 'required substantial computer memory and took several days'. That is numerical computation, not an AI system. Her earlier work on equidistribution is arXiv:2309.00425 (v3 Feb 2025, accepted in Advances in Mathematics).
events.delivers: A bound on consecutive-prime gaps: liminf (p_{n+1} - p_n) at most 240. Not about quadruplets.
events.doubts: No verification statement found. The emergentmind page of the paper notes that the supplied text ends during the proof of a proposition, although its 'Knowledge Gaps' section is site-generated, not the author's. The PDF was not read.
events.direction: Improves the consecutive-gap bound. Orthogonal to the bullet.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math published, on 17 Aug 2026, an interactive Lean 4 blueprint and library (PrimeGapsLib, primegaps.axiommath.ai) formalising Maynard's 2013 paper and the part of Polymath 8b needed for liminf at most 246. The site attributes the Lean proofs to 'AxiomProver', which it describes as 'Axiom Math's AI system for mathematical research through formal proof'. The blueprint states the formalisation assumes only Bombieri-Vinogradov. The site calls the work a reconstruction, not a new theorem. The blueprint PDF was not read; a search excerpt lists seven authors, while a news report says 41 named contributors.
events.delivers: A machine-checked, conditional (on Bombieri-Vinogradov) version of the 246 bound, which Polymath 8b established in 2014. It adds no new bound.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks. The result is about consecutive-gap bounds and does not reach quadruplets.

disputes.summary: Stadlmann's 240 and OpenAI's 186. The OpenAI preprint is reported (by a search excerpt of the PDF) to say that Stadlmann independently proved 240. Science News reports that OpenAI said it was in touch with Maynard but did not contact Stadlmann directly, and quotes Granville as saying OpenAI did not 'carefully consider how they treated her'. Recorded, not resolved.

Which bound is the current record for liminf of consecutive prime gaps is contested across sources. A tracker reports Tao's optimisation-problems page as listing 186 as the best known bound (secondary; Tao's page was not opened). Axiom and Charton (212, 3 Sept) and Song and Yue (236, 4 Sept) appear after the 186 preprint's announcement, and the 236 paper does not cite the 212 or 186 results (per a summary). One aggregator says 'Axiom Math lowered the bound from 240 to 212', while another says 246 had stood for twelve years. A Chinese-language report gives 246 as the prior record.
Authorship of the Axiom 246 blueprint. The PDF's author line (per a search excerpt) lists seven names; a news report gives 41 named contributors. Not resolved; the PDF was not read.

summary: Searches (39 web queries, two arXiv listing queries, and about 50 pages opened or attempted) found no proof, disproof, or accepted claim about the infinitude of prime quadruplets from 26 Jan 2024 to 11 Oct 2026, and no AI system tied to the quadruplet pattern. The quadruplet-specific items are: a finite 2026 census of quadruplets for a polynomial (Chen, Zenodo; single author, unrefereed; finite, so it cannot settle infinitude); a 2026 conditional implication (Choudhury and Wei, arXiv:2606.10331: infinitude follows if the authors' characterisation conjecture holds and there are infinitely many solutions, and neither premise is established); and older unrefereed claims (Liberati 2015 IRIS records, whose full text returned HTTP 403 and was read only as search snippets; Tan 2011 Collatz paper with a 'Theorem of prime quadruplets' seen only in a search excerpt). The unconditional classical state is unchanged: Forbes (2000) records only the partial result on (p+2)(p+6)(p+8) having at most 14 prime factors, and Wikipedia still says the question is open. The 2026 activity in the neighbourhood is on the smallest gap H1 between consecutive primes, which moved from 246 (Polymath 8b, 2014) to 240 (Stadlmann, 31 Aug 2026), 236 (Song and Yue, 4 Sept), 212 (Charton et al., 3 Sept, with AxiomProver credited with formal verification and a 'human-AI collaboration' per an aggregator) and 186 (OpenAI, dated 30 Aug and announced 3 Sept, credited to 'GPT 6 Astra'), together with Axiom's Lean formalisation of the 246 bound (17 Aug). These are recorded as events because they are the AI-attributed prime-tuple neighbourhood. None of them concerns the pattern {p, p+2, p+6, p+8}: a bound on the smallest gaps between consecutive primes does not say that all four of p, p+2, p+6, p+8 are prime infinitely often, and Maynard's positive-proportion theorem concerns families of large admissible tuples, not this tuple. The close call is the reading of Maynard's abstract sentence ('the prime k-tuples conjecture holds for a positive proportion of admissible k-tuples'), which the 2024 Baghdad claim repeats. Read literally as all-prime, it would be far stronger than Maynard's theorem; read as some-but-not-all, it is the weak form the search excerpt describes. The paper body was not read, so I record both readings and do not choose. Two AI-credited results are not checked against their primary PDFs, which WebFetch could not read (binary). The OpenAI quotation 'The proof is due to GPT 6 Astra' comes from a search excerpt of that PDF. The 'Prime gaps at most 182' manuscript credited to GPT-6 Astra was not on the page cited for it and is recorded as unverified. The 2026 record is incomplete on primary text and is recorded as such in incomplete.
competing_reading: The bounded-gap wave is the nearest active programme, and the methods behind it (Maynard-Tao sieves, Polymath-style equidistribution) do give infinitely many n with several of the linear forms prime. A reader who treats the 186 and 212 results as progress on k-tuples would be using the method family as the problem's family. The bullet asks about the all-four pattern {0,2,6,8}, and none of the 2026 results reaches it. A second reading: the 2024 Baghdad claim and Maynard's abstract could be read as already settling a positive-proportion version of the all-prime conjecture for a class of tuples that includes {0,2,6,8}. The record does not support that, because neither source names this tuple and the literal all-prime reading of 'positive proportion' is in doubt.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A proof that infinitely many n make n, n+2, n+6 and n+8 all prime, or a published proof of the prime k-tuples conjecture for {0,2,6,8}. (2) Reading the OpenAI short-gaps PDF and Axiom's bgp212.pdf to confirm whether either mentions the four-element tuple {0,2,6,8}, and to fix each system's role in its argument. (3) Reading the body of Maynard's 2013 paper to fix the meaning of 'holds for a positive proportion', and then reading the Baghdad 2024 paper against it. (4) Access to the CNR full texts of the Liberati records, the Tan Collatz PDF's quadruplet section, and the Chen census quadruplet list, which can be tested with a primality test. (5) A signed reply from Maynard or Tao on whether the 186 and 212 methods reach any tuple of size four.

dead_ends: No proof, disproof or accepted claim of infinitude for {p, p+2, p+6, p+8} in any 2024-2026 source, in the queries above.

No AI system (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, Gemini Deep Think, ChatGPT, Claude) found credited with any quadruplet result. A 2025 DeepMind/Tao/Gomez-Serrano paper (arXiv:2511.02864, 67 problems) appears in search; its number-theory items were not shown to involve prime tuples, and it was not opened.
OpenAI 'Ten advances' (1 Aug 2026): nine of the ten items were visible in excerpts, none about primes; the tenth was not found. Not a source for this bullet.

Erdos Problem #1196 (GPT-5.4 Pro, April 2026, primitive sets) concerns primitive sets, not prime tuples. Erdos Problem #890 forum thread uses the k-tuples conjecture as a conditional tool for a composite-run question; not an event for this bullet.
No Lean or Mathlib formalisation of the quadruplet statement found. Formalisations found concern consecutive-gap bounds only (Axiom 246; OpenAI 186).
'Prime gaps at most 182' (GPT-6 Astra, UCLA listing): the cited page does not contain it.

Halberstam-Richert (Sieve Methods, 1974) is the usual source named for sieve bounds on prime tuples; the specific (p+2)(p+6)(p+8) statement was not found in the book's search excerpts. The origin of the 14-factor statement is unresolved.

Cai (2017, Acta Arithmetica 179): infinitely many primes p with p+2 having at most 2 and p+6 at most 14 prime factors. Seen in search only, a pair-level almost-prime result, not an event for this bullet.
Heath-Brown and Li (2015) and Porter/Maynard results on n(n+2)(n+6) with few prime factors: seen in search, almost-prime statements, not events.
Zhang (2014), Polymath 8b (2014) bounded-gap bounds: background to the consecutive-gap events, not events for this bullet.
Tao-Ziegler 'Ascending chains of prime-producing tuples' (2023, J. Anal. Math.): an existence result for some prime-producing tuples, not {0,2,6,8}; seen in search, not opened, predates the window.
Robles-Perez and Rosales, arXiv:2112.05501 (Frobenius problem from prime k-tuplets, 2021): a numerical-semigroup problem motivated by quadruplets, not a result on infinitude; seen in listing only.

Polignac-type 2026 Zenodo claims (a 'Fixed-Window Tower Sieve' Polignac proof, June 2026, multiple versions): these concern Polignac's conjecture, which implies no particular quadruplet result, and were not opened. Recorded here so the denominator shows they were seen.

incomplete: Primary text was not readable for several key items, so the record rests on abstract pages, search excerpts and secondary coverage for them: (a) the OpenAI 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes' PDF (binary; the 'The proof is due to GPT 6 Astra' quote and the 30 Aug date come from search excerpts; the OpenAI page returned 403); (b) Axiom's 'A New Bound for Small Gaps Between Primes' PDF (binary), so the 212 argument, its Lean scope and the division of labour are unverified; (c) the Axiom blueprint and paper pages (too large to fetch); (d) the Song-Yue ePrint PDF and the Choudhury-Wei PDF (abstract pages only); (e) the Stadlmann PDF (abstract page and a third-party summary only); (f) the body of Maynard's 2013 paper, so the meaning of 'holds for a positive proportion' is not settled; (g) the Tan Collatz PDF's quadruplet section (search excerpt only); (h) both Liberati IRIS records (HTTP 403; search snippets only); (i) the Mor and Gupta 2024 paper (DNS failure; search excerpts only, and its month is unknown); (j) the Zhu 2025 paper (EBSCO record and a secondary citation only); (k) Pratt 2024 and Leung 2024 (titles and listing only; not opened); (l) Tao's optimisation-problems page and Mathstodon post (not opened; the 'Tao lists 186' statement is secondary); (m) X posts by Weijie Su and Ashvin Swaminathan (not opened; the Su attribution could not be located at all); (n) the 'Improved Long Gaps' companion (not read); (o) the Chen census quadruplet list and the Part I Zenodo record 18701355 (not checked); (p) Halberstam-Richert's book and the origin of the 14-factor result (not located). None of these gaps bears on whether the quadruplet question has been resolved, since no source in the record claims that, but they limit how precisely the bounded-gap events and their AI involvement can be read.
